items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations are expressed in units of W/m2.
items.Rationale: The prompt explicitly specifies incident flux in W/m2 as the required unit.
items.Citation: Parametric equations of incident flux [w/m2]

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations are expressed as functions of an orbital time or true anomaly parameter T.
items.Rationale: The prompt asks for parametric equations of flux, and the subsequent plot requirement confirms T is the independent variable; equations must be explicit functions of T.
items.Citation: incident flux on each face of the satellite vs T

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations account for eclipse periods where incident solar flux drops to zero.
items.Rationale: In any low Earth orbit, eclipse is a fundamental boundary condition. Correct parametric equations must include piecewise or eclipse-angle-based terms that zero out solar flux during shadow passages.

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations include a solar flux component derived from the solar constant or equivalent direct solar irradiance.
items.Rationale: Incident flux on a satellite face in LEO has three components: direct solar, Earth albedo, and Earth infrared. Solar flux from the solar constant is the dominant term and must appear in the equations.

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations include an Earth albedo flux component.
items.Rationale: Earth albedo is a standard thermal boundary condition for LEO satellites and must be included in any complete parametric flux analysis.

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations include an Earth infrared (OLR) flux component.
items.Rationale: Earth-emitted infrared (outgoing longwave radiation) is the third standard thermal boundary input for LEO satellites and is required for completeness.

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations incorporate the beta angle to determine the illumination geometry relative to the orbit plane.
items.Rationale: Beta angle is the angle between the sun vector and the orbit plane and is the fundamental parameter governing which faces are illuminated and for how long in a sun-synchronous orbit.

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations use view factors to scale the Earth-emitted and albedo contributions on each face.
items.Rationale: View factors from each satellite face to Earth are required to correctly partition Earth-sourced fluxes in the thermal model; their use in equations is a domain standard.

items.Criterion: The thermal report includes a plot of incident flux vs T for the worst hot case scenario.
items.Rationale: The prompt explicitly requires flux vs T plots for both worst hot and worst cold cases.
items.Citation: incident flux on each face of the satellite vs T for the worst hot case and the worst cold case scenarios

items.Criterion: The thermal report includes a plot of incident flux vs T for the worst cold case scenario.
items.Rationale: The prompt explicitly requires flux vs T plots for both worst hot and worst cold cases.
items.Citation: incident flux on each face of the satellite vs T for the worst hot case and the worst cold case scenarios

items.Criterion: The worst hot case and worst cold case scenarios are selected from across all days in 2028.
items.Rationale: The prompt requires identification of worst cases among all the days in 2028, not just a single representative day.
items.Citation: worst hot case and the worst cold case scenarios among all the days in 2028

items.Criterion: The worst hot case is identified as the orbital day or period with maximum total incident flux.
items.Rationale: Worst hot case in orbital thermal analysis is the scenario where the satellite receives maximum heat input; correct identification requires surveying beta angles and solar distances across the year.

items.Criterion: The worst cold case is identified as the orbital day or period with minimum total incident flux.
items.Rationale: Worst cold case is where the satellite receives minimum heat input, typically maximum eclipse or perihelion-minimizing geometry; correct identification is required by the prompt.

items.Criterion: The flux vs T plots show all six satellite faces on either a single plot per scenario or clearly labeled separate subplots.
items.Rationale: The prompt asks for flux on each face vs T, implying all six faces must be represented in each scenario plot.
items.Citation: incident flux on each face of the satellite vs T

items.Criterion: The flux vs T plots show eclipse regions where flux goes to zero during shadow passage.
items.Rationale: A correct flux vs T plot for a LEO sun-synchronous orbit must show eclipse intervals where solar flux on illuminated faces drops to zero; absence indicates an incomplete or incorrect model.

items.Criterion: The flux vs T plots display the T axis over at least one complete orbital period.
items.Rationale: A parametric analysis of flux vs orbital parameter T must span a full orbit to be meaningful as a boundary condition deliverable.

items.Criterion: The summary table in the thermal report includes view factors for the satellite faces.
items.Rationale: The prompt explicitly lists view factors as required parameters in the summary table.
items.Citation: View factors

items.Criterion: The summary table is presented for both the worst hot case and worst cold case scenarios separately.
items.Rationale: The prompt asks for key parameter values for worst case scenarios (plural), requiring the table to cover both hot and cold cases.
items.Citation: Give the important parameter values ... for worst case scenarios

items.Criterion: The beta angle value stated in the summary table is consistent with the beta angle used in the parametric flux equations.
items.Rationale: Internal consistency check: the beta angle driving the flux model must match the beta angle reported in the summary table; inconsistency indicates a calculation error.

items.Criterion: The eclipse angle stated in the summary table is geometrically consistent with the orbital altitude and beta angle reported for that case.
items.Rationale: Eclipse angle, orbital altitude, and beta angle are mathematically related; a correct thermal analysis must maintain consistency among these three parameters.

items.Criterion: The view factors in the summary table for Earth-facing and space-facing faces are distinct and reflect the satellite geometry relative to Earth.
items.Rationale: For a 10x10x10 cm cube in LEO, the face pointing nadir has a larger view factor to Earth than zenith and lateral faces; reporting identical view factors for all faces would indicate an error.

items.Criterion: The sum of view factors from any single satellite face to Earth and to deep space is less than or equal to 1.
items.Rationale: View factor reciprocity and completeness relations require that for any flat surface, the combined view factor to all surrounding surfaces cannot exceed 1; this is a fundamental domain constraint.

items.Criterion: The maximum flux value reported for any face does not exceed the solar constant (approximately 1414 W/m2 for closest Earth-Sun distance).
items.Rationale: The solar constant at 1 AU is approximately 1361 W/m2, peaking near 1414 W/m2 at perihelion; no face can receive more direct solar flux than this physical upper bound.

items.Criterion: The minimum incident flux on any face during an illuminated orbital phase is greater than zero.
items.Rationale: During the sunlit portion of an orbit, Earth IR and albedo always contribute a positive flux to all faces; a zero minimum outside eclipse indicates an incomplete model.

items.Criterion: The Qsun value in the summary table is consistent with the solar flux incident on the satellite's cross-sectional area facing the sun.
items.Rationale: Qsun (total incident solar power) must be derivable from the projected area of the satellite facing the sun and the solar irradiance; the reported value must align with this calculation.

items.Criterion: The worst hot case corresponds to a positive beta angle condition where the sun is above the orbit plane, resulting in longer sunlit periods.
items.Rationale: In sun-synchronous orbit, the worst hot case typically occurs at high positive beta angles where eclipse fraction decreases; the report must identify this condition correctly.

items.Criterion: The worst cold case corresponds to a condition with a long eclipse fraction, typically at or near zero beta angle.
items.Rationale: In sun-synchronous orbit, maximum eclipse occurs near zero beta angle, producing the coldest thermal environment; the report must correctly identify this geometry.

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations are dimensionally consistent, with coefficients and terms that produce units of W/m2.
items.Rationale: Dimensional consistency is a fundamental correctness requirement; equations that mix units or produce wrong dimensions are professionally unusable.

items.Criterion: The parametric flux equations for opposite faces (such as +Z and -Z) sum to a value that does not exceed the total available flux input from the solar and Earth sources.
items.Rationale: Energy conservation requires that the total flux distributed across all faces must not exceed total available incident power; inconsistency across opposite faces indicates modeling error.

items.Criterion: The flux vs T plots include labeled axes with T on the horizontal axis and incident flux in W/m2 on the vertical axis.
items.Rationale: Properly labeled axes are a minimum formatting requirement for a professional engineering plot; unlabeled plots are unusable by ABC Survey engineers.

items.Criterion: The flux vs T plots include a legend identifying which curve corresponds to which satellite face.
items.Rationale: A legend is required when multiple faces are plotted together; without it, the curves cannot be distinguished and the plot is not usable as a thermal boundary condition.

items.Criterion: The summary table is formatted with clearly labeled columns identifying the parameter name, the worst hot case value, and the worst cold case value.
items.Rationale: A professional engineering report table must have labeled columns so that ABC Survey engineers can extract correct values without ambiguity.

items.Criterion: The beta angle values reported in the summary table are within the physically possible range for a sun-synchronous orbit in 2028.
items.Rationale: For a sun-synchronous orbit, the beta angle varies within a bounded range determined by the inclination and solar declination; values outside this range indicate a calculation error.

items.Criterion: The eclipse angle (ec) reported in the summary table is expressed in degrees and falls within the range 0 to 90 degrees.
items.Rationale: Eclipse angle is the half-angle of Earth's shadow cone as seen from the orbit; it is bounded between 0 and 90 degrees, and values outside this range indicate a definitional or computational error.

items.Criterion: The flux equations or accompanying text account for the variation in Earth-Sun distance throughout 2028 when computing solar irradiance.
items.Rationale: Solar irradiance varies by approximately plus or minus 3.3% due to Earth's orbital eccentricity over a year; a complete parametric thermal analysis for all days in 2028 must address this variation.

items.Criterion: The thermal report applies orbital mechanics specific to sun-synchronous orbit, including the frozen repeat ground track or retrograde inclination near 97-98 degrees.
items.Rationale: Sun-synchronous orbits have a characteristic retrograde inclination chosen to maintain a fixed sun angle; a report that treats the orbit as a generic circular orbit rather than acknowledging SSO-specific properties is incomplete.

items.Criterion: The thermal report does not contain placeholder text such as TBD, TODO, or INSERT VALUE HERE.
items.Rationale: Placeholder text in a deliverable submitted to ABC Survey indicates an incomplete analysis that is not ready for use as a thermal boundary condition.

items.Criterion: The incident flux equations for a satellite face that is always in shadow (never directly illuminated by the sun for a given beta angle) correctly assign zero solar flux to that face.
items.Rationale: Depending on the beta angle, some faces of the satellite may receive no direct solar illumination during parts of the orbit; correctly zeroing solar contribution on those faces is a domain-critical correctness check.

items.Criterion: The summary table flux values for each face are consistent with the maximum values visually identifiable in the corresponding flux vs T plots.
items.Rationale: Internal consistency: the max/min values in the summary table must match the peaks and troughs shown in the flux vs T plots; discrepancies would make the report internally contradictory.
